title: Eigenspaces and geometric multiplicity
terms: eigenspace; geometric multiplicity; zero eigenspace; independent eigenvectors.

exposition.text:
The eigenspace for λ is E = ker(A − λI), consisting of all corresponding eigenvectors together
λ
with zero. Its dimension is the geometric multiplicity. For an eigenvalue, this dimension is at
least one and no greater than its algebraic multiplicity.
Find an eigenspace by row-reducing A − λI. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly
independent, but repeated roots do not guarantee enough independent eigenvectors to form a
basis. The zero eigenspace is exactly the nullspace. An eigenvalue can have algebraic multiplic-
ity three and geometric multiplicity only one.
Eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues have zero intersection and their sum is direct. If v = u + w
with Au = λu, Aw = µw, and λ ̸= µ, then u = (Av − µv)/(λ − µ). This isolates an eigenspace
component without finding all coordinates of an eigenbasis.

question.text:
A 4 × 4 matrix has distinct eigenvalues 1, 2, 3, with eigenspace dimensions 2, 1, 1 respectively.
What is its determinant?
(A) 6 (B) 12 (C) 18 (D) 24 (E) Cannot be determined

solution.text:
The eigenspaces provide four independent eigenvectors, hence a basis. The eigenvalues in
that basis are 1, 1, 2, 3, so their product is 6.

question.text:
A 4 × 4 matrix has exactly one distinct eigenvalue, namely 2, and a two-dimensional eigenspace.
Is it diagonalizable?
(A) Yes
(B) The data are insufficient
(C) Only if its trace is zero
(D) No
(E) Only if its determinant is nonzero

solution.text:
Diagonalizability requires four independent eigenvectors. With only one eigenvalue, all
eigenvectors lie in its two-dimensional eigenspace, so there cannot be an eigenbasis.

question.text:
Suppose v = u + w, where Au = 2u and Aw = 5w. Which expression recovers u from v and Av?
(A) (Av − 2v)/3 (B) (5v − Av)/3 (C) (Av − 5v)/3 (D) (2v + Av)/7 (E) (5Av − v)/3

solution.text:
From Av = 2u + 5w and 5v = 5u + 5w, subtraction gives 5v − Av = 3u. Distinct eigenvalues
allow separate eigenspace components to be isolated by a polynomial in the operator.

question.text:
An eigenvalue has algebraic multiplicity three. Which is impossible for its geometric multiplic-
ity?
(A) All of 1, 2, 3 are impossible
(B) 3
(C) 4
(D) 2
(E) 1

solution.text:
Geometric multiplicity is at least one and at most algebraic multiplicity. The values one,
two, and three can all occur, according to the Jordan block structure; four cannot.
